mainTopic: What wage a worker in a half-profit deal (storekeeper, animal raiser) must receive so it is not רבית, and how much counts as a wage.
overview: The משנה taught that a storekeeper (חנווני) who sells your goods, or buys produce with your money, for half the profit must be paid a wage. Otherwise his extra work counts as רבית. אביי explains that the wage is כפועל בטל: what a worker in his own trade would accept to give up his usual work for this lighter job. The גמרא explains why the משנה needed both cases, and then gives a memory sign for the topics that follow. A ברייתא brings three views on how much the wage must be: any agreed amount (רבי מאיר), even a tiny benefit (רבי יהודה), or a full wage (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי). The same question decides arguments about raising goats and sheep, a chicken sitting on another woman's eggs, and a calf or foal raised with its mother. In those cases the lenient side points to small benefits like whey, unhatched eggs, or dung. רב נחמן rules like the lenient opinions. The amud ends with a contract of רב עילִישׁ that splits profit and loss in half. רבא begins to show it must have meant a permitted deal, and his argument continues on the next amud.

steps.title: אביי defines the 'idle worker' wage
steps.stepSummary: אביי explains that the wage of a פועל בטל is measured against the specific trade the person is giving up.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: He is paid like an idle worker of that same type of work that he is kept idle from.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי explains what 'paid like an idle worker' means: the amount a person in this storekeeper's own trade would accept to give up his usual work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Idle worker' does not mean full wages, and it does not mean a random small amount. It is measured by the person's own trade: how much a worker of that kind would take to skip his normal, harder job and do this lighter task. So the payment changes depending on what work he is giving up.

keyTerms.meaning: An idle worker: the pay a worker would accept to sit out his usual work
Work, a trade or type of labor
That he is kept idle from, the work he is giving up

phrases.english: Abaye said:
Like an idle worker
of that same type of work
that he is kept idle from.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: כְּפוֹעֵל בָּטֵל שֶׁל אוֹתָהּ מְלָאכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the term כפועל בטל, which was used just before this point as the measure of the storekeeper's wage.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The wage of a פועל בטל is what a worker of that specific trade would accept to give up his usual work for this lighter job.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical amount the investor must pay so that the half-profit deal does not become רבית.

steps.title: Why the storekeeper case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a צריכותא: if the משנה had taught only the חנווני case, we might think the money-to-buy-produce case needs more pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And both cases are needed. If the משנה had taught only the storekeeper, I would say it is the storekeeper for whom idle-worker pay is enough, because his effort is not great. But someone given money to buy produce, whose effort is great, I would say idle-worker pay is not enough for him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts explaining why the משנה listed two cases. This step shows what we could wrongly conclude if only the חנווני case had been written.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חנווני already has the goods in hand and only needs to sell them, so his effort is small. The person given money must go out, find the produce and bring it back, which is much more work. From the חנווני case alone, we might think the harder job needs more than idle-worker pay, so the משנה had to teach the money case too.

keyTerms.meaning: It is necessary: the גמרא explains why two cases both had to be taught
His effort or bother is great
Money given to buy produce with

phrases.english: And it is necessary [to teach both cases],
for if the משנה had taught only the storekeeper:
it is a storekeeper for whom it is enough
to be paid like an idle worker,
because his effort is not great.
But one given money to buy produce with,
whose effort is great –

phrases.aramaic: אֵימָא לָא סַגִּי לֵיהּ כְּפוֹעֵל בָּטֵל.
phrases.english: I would say idle-worker pay is not enough for him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּצְרִיכָא, דְּאִי תְּנָא חֶנְוָנִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After defining the wage, the גמרא explains why the משנה needed both the storekeeper case and the money case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without the money case, we might think a harder job needs more than idle-worker pay.
steps.confusionAlert: The 'I would say' here is a mistaken guess that the גמרא brings up and then sets aside. It is NOT the הלכה: in both cases idle-worker pay is the rule.

steps.title: Why the money case alone would not be enough
steps.stepSummary: The other side of the צריכותא: from the money case alone, we might think a storekeeper needs only a token payment. So both cases are necessary.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had taught only money to buy produce, I would have said: there he needs idle-worker pay, because his effort is great. But a storekeeper, whose effort is not great, I would say any small amount is enough for him, so that even if the owner only dipped bread with him in brine, or only ate one dried fig with him, that is his pay. Therefore both are necessary.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the opposite mistake: from the money case alone, we might think the storekeeper needs only a tiny token payment. It concludes that both cases are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If only the harder money case were written, we might think idle-worker pay is needed only because the effort is great. Then the חנווני, whose job is easy, might be paid with almost nothing, like a dip in brine or one fig. By writing both cases, the משנה teaches that idle-worker pay is the measure in both: not more for the hard job, and not less for the easy one.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have said: a mistaken first guess
Brine, fish sauce used for dipping bread

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי תְּנָא מָעוֹת לִיקַּח בָּהֶן פֵּירוֹת –
phrases.english: And if the משנה had taught only money to buy produce with –
I would have said:
it is there that he needs idle-worker pay,
because his effort is great.
But a storekeeper, whose effort is not great –
I would say any small amount is enough for him,

phrases.aramaic: דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֹא טִבֵּל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא בְּצִיר,
phrases.english: so that even if he only dipped [his bread] with him in brine,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָכַל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא גְּרוֹגֶרֶת אַחַת –
phrases.english: or only ate one dried fig with him –
this is his pay,
[therefore] both are necessary.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי תְּנָא מָעוֹת לִיקַּח בָּהֶן פֵּירוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the צריכותא started in step 2 by giving the opposite mistaken guess, then concludes that both cases are needed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Idle-worker pay is the fixed measure in both cases: the harder money job does not need more, and the easy storekeeper job cannot get by with a token payment.
steps.whatToRemember: Under the rules of רבית, a half-profit worker must get a real wage, כפועל בטל of his own trade. This applies equally whether he sells goods (חנווני) or buys produce with the money.

steps.title: A memory sign for the next discussions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a list of key words (how many, goats, chickens, we add) to help remember the order of the upcoming סוגיות.
steps.simpleTranslation: (How many, goats, and chickens, we add: a memory sign.)
steps.whatsHappening: This is not a new argument. The גמרא is setting up the next part of the דף by giving a short memory sign for the topics coming up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each key word points to an upcoming discussion: 'how many' (how much pay), 'goats,' 'chickens,' and 'we add.' These help a learner remember the order of the next סוגיות, which all deal with similar half-profit deals.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory sign: key words that help you remember the order of topics
We add or raise, here the key word for an upcoming topic

phrases.english: (How many, goats, and chickens,
phrases.notes: This line is a memory sign, not part of the argument. Some versions have the words in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: we add: a memory sign.)

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּמָּה עִיזֵּי וְתַרְנְגוֹלִין מַעֲלִין סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A transition. The צריכותא is finished, and this memory sign introduces a new set of related discussions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No ruling. It is a memory aid listing the upcoming topics.

steps.title: How much must the storekeeper be paid
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא gives three opinions on the minimum wage for the חנווני: רבי מאיר says any agreed amount, רבי יהודה says even a tiny benefit, and רבי שמעון בן יוחאי says a full worker's wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: How much is his wage? Whether a lot or a little, says רבי מאיר. רבי יהודה says: even if he only dipped his bread in brine with him, or ate one dried fig with him, that is his wage. רבי שמעון בן יוחאי says: he gives him his full wage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that asks how much the storekeeper from the משנה must be paid so the partnership is not ריבית.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the storekeeper must get a wage but did not say how much. רבי מאיר lets them agree on any amount. רבי יהודה is the most lenient: even a tiny benefit like a dip of brine counts. רבי שמעון בן יוחאי is the strictest: he requires a real, full wage.

keyTerms.meaning: Brine, a cheap salty liquid for dipping bread
A dried fig, a very small food item

phrases.english: The Sages taught: How much is his wage?
phrases.notes: "His" means the storekeeper from our משנה, who must get paid for his work.

phrases.english: Whether a lot or a little,
these are the words of Rabbi Meir.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא טִבֵּל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא בְּצִיר,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: Even if he only dipped with him in brine,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָכַל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא גְּרוֹגֶרֶת אַחַת –
phrases.english: and only ate one dried fig with him,
that is his wage.
Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai says:
He gives him his full wage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: כַּמָּה הוּא שְׂכָרוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the first topic from the memory list (כמה) in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three views on the minimum wage: any agreed amount (רבי מאיר), even a token benefit (רבי יהודה), a full worker's wage (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי).

steps.title: No appraising goats or sheep for half the profit
steps.stepSummary: A second ברייתא: one may not give goats, sheep, or any animal that does not produce while it eats to someone to raise for half the profit.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: One may not appraise goats or sheep, or anything that does not work while it eats, for half.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about handing animals to someone to raise, splitting the increase in value.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The raiser works and feeds the animal but only gets paid later out of the shared profit. If the animal gives him nothing along the way, his work looks like a payment to the owner for the money he is holding, which is ריבית. So the תנא קמא forbids this for goats and sheep.

keyTerms.meaning: Appraise, set a value on an animal handed over for raising
Works while it eats, meaning it produces something while being fed

steps.confusionAlert: Goats and sheep obviously do give milk and wool. The תנא קמא is not denying that. The גמרא will explain his reasoning in steps 8 and 9.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One may not appraise
phrases.notes: This means setting a value on an animal, giving it to someone to raise, and splitting any rise in its value.

phrases.aramaic: לֹא אֶת הָעִזִּים וְלֹא אֶת הָרְחֵלִים,
phrases.english: neither goats nor sheep,
nor anything
that does not work while it eats, for half.
phrases.notes: "For half" goes back to "appraise": the deal where the raiser gets half the profit.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: אֵין שָׁמִין לֹא אֶת הָעִזִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the second topic from the memory list (עזים) in step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The תנא קמא forbids appraising goats, sheep, or any non-producing animal for half the profit.

steps.title: רבי יוסי permits goats, sheep and chickens
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה permits the arrangement for goats (milk), sheep (wool from shearing, washing, plucking) and chickens (eggs), because they produce while they eat.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי son of רבי יהודה says: One may appraise goats because they give milk, sheep because they are shorn, washed and plucked, and a chicken because it works while it eats.
steps.whatsHappening: A dissenting opinion in the ברייתא says these animals may be appraised for half the profit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה reasons that the milk, wool and eggs the raiser collects along the way count as his wage. Because he is being paid, his work is no longer ריבית.

keyTerms.meaning: They are washed, and wool comes off
They are plucked, and wool is pulled off

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says:
One may appraise goats because they give milk,
and sheep because they are shorn
and washed and plucked,
phrases.notes: Wool comes off when sheep are washed or brush against thorns, and the raiser can collect it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֶת הַתַּרְנְגוֹלֶת מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהִיא עוֹשָׂה וְאוֹכֶלֶת.
phrases.english: and a chicken because it works while it eats.
phrases.notes: It lays eggs while being fed.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: שָׁמִין אֶת הָעִזִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The opposing view within the same ברייתא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Animals that produce milk, wool or eggs may be appraised, since that produce serves as the raiser's wage.

steps.title: Why doesn't the first opinion count wool and milk as payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how the תנא קמא can hold that wool and milk are not enough to pay for the raiser's work and the animal's food.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the first תנא: do shearing and milk not cover the pay for his work and the food?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the תנא קמא: wool and milk seem like plenty of payment, so why does he forbid the deal?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי's reasoning seems obvious, since the raiser clearly gets milk and wool. The גמרא wants to know what the תנא קמא could possibly answer. This sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: The first (anonymous) opinion in the ברייתא

phrases.english: And the first תנא:
do shearing and milk not cover
the pay for his work and the food?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְתַנָּא קַמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the תנא קמא's position in light of רבי יוסי's reasoning.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the תנא קמא's reason for forbidding, when wool and milk seem to be a sufficient wage?

steps.title: The dispute is only about whey and plucked tufts
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees wool and milk are a sufficient wage. They argue only when the raiser gets just the whey and the plucked bits.
steps.simpleTranslation: With wool and milk, everyone agrees. Where they argue is about whey and pluckings.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by narrowing the argument: if the raiser keeps the wool and milk, all agree the deal is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is only when the owner keeps the real wool and milk, and the raiser gets just the leftovers: whey, the watery liquid left after making cheese, and loose tufts of plucked wool. The תנא קמא says those leftovers are too small to count as a wage. רבי יוסי says they are enough.

keyTerms.meaning: Whey, the watery leftover of milk

steps.whatToRemember: Appraising animals for half the profit is allowed if the raiser gets real produce like milk and wool. The argument is only over whether leftovers like whey and plucked tufts are enough of a wage.

phrases.aramaic: בְּגִיזָּה וְחָלָב – כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי,
phrases.english: With wool and milk, everyone agrees,
phrases.notes: He means when the raiser gets to keep the wool and milk.

phrases.english: where they argue is about whey and pluckings.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּגִיזָּה וְחָלָב – כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8 by redefining the case in dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) of the dispute
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנא קמא forbids even when the raiser receives the wool and milk.
steps.terutzMaskana: All permit when the raiser gets the wool and milk. They argue only when he gets just the whey and plucked tufts.

steps.title: Each side of the argument follows an earlier opinion about the wage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא links the argument about whey and plucked bits to the earlier ברייתא. The תנא קמא follows רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, who requires a full wage. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה follows his father, רבי יהודה, who says even a tiny benefit is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא קמא holds like רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, who says the worker must get his full wage. רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה holds like his father, who says that even dipping bread in brine with him, or eating one dried fig with him, counts as his wage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its answer from step 9. It shows that each side of the argument about whey and plucked bits matches an opinion we already saw in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Whey and plucked bits are worth much less than a full wage. That is not enough for רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, so the תנא קמא forbids the deal. For רבי יהודה any small benefit is a wage, so his son permits it.

keyTerms.meaning: his full wage, the real pay a worker would normally get
brine, salty fish-juice used for dipping bread

steps.whatToRemember: The argument about goats and sheep comes down to one question: must the raiser get a full wage (רבי שמעון בן יוחאי), or is any small benefit enough (רבי יהודה)?
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties the animal-raising case back to the general rule about a wage, which keeps the עיסקא partnership from becoming ריבית.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא קַמָּא סָבַר לַהּ כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי,
phrases.english: The first tanna holds like Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai,
who says: he gives him his full wage.
phrases.notes: This is the opinion from the ברייתא in step 5.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה סָבַר לַהּ כַּאֲבוּהּ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda holds like his father,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ לֹא טִבֵּל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא בְּצִיר,
phrases.english: who says: even if he only dipped his bread in brine with him,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא אָכַל עִמּוֹ אֶלָּא גְּרוֹגֶרֶת אַחַת –
phrases.english: and only ate one dried fig with him,
this is his wage.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנָּא קַמָּא סָבַר לַהּ כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the answer of step 9 by naming the source of each side's view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Matching each side to an earlier opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It looked as if the תנא קמא held that even wool and milk are not a wage.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both sides agree wool and milk are enough. They argue only about whey and plucked bits, and that argument depends on whether a full wage is required.

steps.title: Renting out a chicken in exchange for two chicks
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a woman may rent out her chicken to sit on her friend's eggs, and be paid with two of the chicks.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: a woman may rent out her chicken to her friend in exchange for two chicks.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about a chicken that sits on eggs. This first case is a simple rental, and it is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a plain rental with a fixed price of two chicks. It is not a shared-risk partnership, so there is no ריבית problem. It sets up the harder case in the next step.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:
A woman may rent out to her friend
a chicken in exchange for two chicks.
phrases.notes: The chicken sits on the friend's eggs, and the chicken's owner gets two of the chicks that hatch as her pay.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מַשְׂכֶּרֶת אִשָּׁה לַחֲבֶרְתָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on a related case of raising for profit.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fixed rental, a chicken for two chicks, is allowed.

steps.title: Splitting the chicks: רבי יהודה permits, רבי שמעון forbids
steps.stepSummary: One woman owns the chicken and the other owns the eggs, and they agree to split the chicks. רבי יהודה permits this and רבי שמעון forbids it.
steps.simpleTranslation: If a woman said to her friend, "The chicken is mine and the eggs are yours, and we will split the chicks," רבי יהודה permits it and רבי שמעון forbids it.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא continues with a partnership instead of a rental. The two תנאים argue about whether it is allowed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This deal works like the half-profit partnership, so the chicken owner needs some kind of wage. רבי שמעון forbids it because she gets no real pay for her chicken's work. רבי יהודה permits it, which fits his view that even a small benefit is enough.

phrases.english: A woman who said to her friend:
"The chicken is mine and the eggs are yours,
and you and I will split the chicks" —

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה מַתִּיר, רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן אוֹסֵר.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda permits, Rabbi Shimon forbids.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִשָּׁה שֶׁאָמְרָה לַחֲבֶרְתָּהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא with a split-the-profits case instead of a fixed rental.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Splitting the chicks is a dispute: רבי יהודה permits it, רבי שמעון forbids it.

steps.title: Does רבי יהודה not require any wage here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: even רבי יהודה requires some small wage, so where is the chicken owner's pay for her work and for the chicken's food?
steps.simpleTranslation: Does רבי יהודה not require pay for her work and for the chicken's food?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יהודה's ruling. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 5 רבי יהודה said even a tiny benefit is enough, but he still needs something. In this deal the chicken owner seems to get nothing beyond her half of the chicks. So how can he permit it?
steps.confusionAlert: רבי יהודה does not say no wage is needed. He says a very small wage is enough, so the question is where that small wage comes from.

phrases.english: And does Rabbi Yehuda not require
pay for the work and the food?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה לָא בָּעֵי שְׂכַר עֲמָלוֹ וּמְזוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יהודה's ruling in step 12, using his own view from step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהודה's permission to split the chicks
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even רבי יהודה needs some small wage, and no wage is visible in this deal.

steps.title: The eggs that never hatch are her wage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that some eggs never hatch, and those go to the chicken owner. That small benefit is her wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: There are eggs that do not hatch.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by pointing to the small benefit the chicken owner does get.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some eggs never hatch, and the chicken owner keeps them. For רבי יהודה, a small benefit like that is enough to count as a wage, so there is no ריבית problem.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יהודה is consistent: a tiny benefit, like the eggs that do not hatch, counts as a wage.

phrases.english: There are eggs that do not hatch.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא בֵּיצִים מוּזָרוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The chicken owner seemed to get no wage at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: She keeps the eggs that do not hatch, and for רבי יהודה that small benefit is enough.

steps.title: Follow local custom about paying for carrying a young animal
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches: where the custom is to add a porter's wage to the money paid for raising an animal, it must be added. We do not change local custom.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages taught: in a place where people usually add a porter's wage to the money for raising an animal, they add it. One does not change the local custom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא about raising animals. Where the local custom gives the raiser extra pay for carrying the animal, that custom is followed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A young animal sometimes has to be carried on the shoulders. Where people normally pay extra for this, the owner must add that amount to the raiser's pay. Local custom decides.

keyTerms.meaning: a porter's wage, pay for carrying on the shoulders

phrases.english: The Sages taught: A place where they were accustomed
to add a porter's wage to the money for an animal —
phrases.notes: The raiser has to carry a young animal on his shoulders, so in some places he gets extra pay for it.

phrases.english: they add it,
and one does not change from the custom of the region.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן: מָקוֹם שֶׁנָּהֲגוּ לְהַעֲלוֹת שְׂכַר כַּתָּף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new ברייתא on another way the raiser can be paid.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where the custom is to add a porter's wage, it must be added. Local custom is not changed.

steps.title: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: value a calf or foal together with its mother
steps.stepSummary: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says one may value a calf with its mother, or a foal with its mother, as one deal. This holds even where the custom is to add a porter's wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: one may value a calf together with its mother, and a foal together with its mother, even in a place where the custom is to add a porter's wage.
steps.whatsHappening: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל adds a case where the porter's-wage custom does not apply: a young animal given over together with its mother.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the calf or foal is raised together with its mother, they can be valued and handled as one deal. The raiser does not get the extra porter's wage, even in a place where that is the custom.
steps.whatToRemember: Local custom about a porter's wage is followed. But according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, a young animal raised with its mother can be valued together with her without that extra pay.

phrases.english: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One may value a calf with its mother,
and a foal with its mother,
and even in a place where they were accustomed
to add a porter's wage to the money.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר: שָׁמִין עֵגֶל עִם אִמּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds an exception to the porter's-wage custom of step 15.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A calf or foal may be valued together with its mother without adding a porter's wage, even where that is the custom.

steps.title: Where is the caretaker's wage in רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבן שמעון בן גמליאל: does he not also require some small pay for the caretaker's work and for the animal's food?
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, does he not require pay for the caretaker's work and food?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question about רבן שמעון בן גמליאל that it asked earlier about רבי יהודה. When a calf is valued together with its mother, where does the caretaker get paid?
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier (step 13) we learned that even the lenient view needs the caretaker to get some small benefit, or the deal looks like ריבית. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allowed the calf to be valued with its mother (step 16), so the גמרא wants to know what benefit pays for the caretaker's effort and feeding.

keyTerms.meaning: Pay for his work and effort
The animal's food, which the caretaker provides

phrases.english: And רבן שמעון בן גמליאל,
does he not require pay for the work and the food?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל לָא בָּעֵי שְׂכַר עֲמָלוֹ וּמְזוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל from step 16, using the same rule that was applied to רבי יהודה in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל's permission to value a calf together with its mother
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Everyone agrees the caretaker needs some wage to avoid ריבית, and none is visible in this deal.

steps.title: The dung is the caretaker's pay
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the animals' dung, which goes to the caretaker, is his small wage.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is the dung.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: the caretaker keeps the animals' dung, and that counts as a small payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Dung was useful, for example as fertilizer, so it has some value. That small benefit is enough to count as the caretaker's wage, so the deal is not ריבית according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

phrases.english: There is the dung.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא גְּלָלִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a hidden benefit that serves as the wage
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The caretaker seemed to get nothing for his work and food.
steps.terutzMaskana: The dung he keeps is his small wage.

steps.title: The other opinion: dung is given up, so it is not a wage
steps.stepSummary: The other sage disagrees because, in his view, people make dung ownerless, so it cannot count as pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the other sage? He holds that people declare the dung ownerless.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the sage who forbids this deal does not accept the dung answer. He says people do not care about dung and give it up, so it is worth nothing as a wage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The other sage does not accept dung as a wage. In his view the dung is simply given up as ownerless, so the caretaker is not really receiving anything from the deal. That is why this opinion does not allow valuing the calf with its mother without the extra pay.

keyTerms.meaning: And the other one (the opposing sage)

phrases.english: And the other sage?
phrases.notes: This is the first opinion in the ברייתא, who disagrees with רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and says to add the porter's wage where that is the custom.

phrases.english: Dung, he declares it ownerless.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִידַּךְ: גְּלָלִים – אַפְקוֹרֵי מַפְקֵיר לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the opposing view rejects the answer of step 18.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Only according to the opposing sage; it explains the disagreement and does not refute רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Dung is usually given up by its owner, so it cannot serve as payment.
steps.whatToRemember: The lenient views find a small hidden wage for the caretaker: unhatched eggs for רבי יהודה, and dung for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. The opposing view says dung is given up as ownerless, so it does not count.

steps.title: רב נחמן rules like all three lenient opinions
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן rules that the הלכה follows רבי יהודה, רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: The הלכה follows רבי יהודה, and it follows רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, and it follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives the practical ruling for these partnership cases. In each one we follow the lenient sage.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of these three sages permitted a type of shared animal or egg deal that another sage forbade. By ruling like all three, רב נחמן makes these deals allowed in practice, as long as the caretaker gets some small benefit.
steps.whatToRemember: In practice, the lenient views stand: the chicken-and-eggs deal, רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה's ruling, and valuing a calf with its mother are all permitted.
steps.whyThisMatters: This turns the debate into practical הלכה for business partnerships involving animals.

phrases.english: רב נחמן said:
The halacha follows רבי יהודה,
phrases.notes: This is the chicken-and-eggs case from step 12.

phrases.english: and the halacha follows רבי יוסי son of רבי יהודה,
and the halacha follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
phrases.notes: This is the calf valued with its mother from step 16.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן: הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the animal-partnership discussion with a practical ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The הלכה follows the lenient opinions of רבי יהודה, רבי יוסי ברבי יהודה, and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.

steps.title: A document of רב עילִישׁ splits profit and loss in half
steps.stepSummary: A document turns up against רב עילִישׁ's sons, saying that profit and loss are split half and half.
steps.simpleTranslation: A document came out against the sons of רב עילִישׁ, in which it was written: half in the profit, half in the loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new story. After רב עילִישׁ died, a business contract he made turned up, and it seems to split profit and loss equally. This sets up the next move.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In an investment deal (עיסקא), the worker who runs the business must get some extra benefit for his work. If he just splits everything half and half, he is working on the investor's share for free, which looks like ריבית. That is the problem the גמרא will deal with next.

phrases.english: The sons of רב עילִישׁ:
a certain document came out against them,
in which it was written:
"Half in the profit, half in the loss."

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּנֵי רַב עִילִישׁ נְפַק עֲלַיְיהוּ הָהוּא שְׁטָרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new case about investment deals, after the animal-partnership discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A contract of רב עילִישׁ appears to split profit and loss equally, which looks like ריבית.

steps.title: רבא: רב עילִישׁ would never cause a forbidden deal
steps.stepSummary: רבא says that רב עילִישׁ was a great man and would not lead people into a forbidden act, so the document cannot mean what it seems to say.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: רב עילִישׁ was a great man, and he would not feed people something forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא defends רב עילִישׁ. Because he was a great man, he would never make a deal that gives someone ריבית. Something must be missing from the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not read the contract at face value. He assumes רב עילִישׁ kept the הלכה, so the half-and-half wording must be short for a deal that was actually permitted. He is about to show how.

keyTerms.meaning: A great man, a great scholar

phrases.english: רבא said:
רב עילִישׁ was a great man,
and he would not feed people something forbidden.
phrases.notes: He means רב עיליש would never let his partner earn ריבית through a deal.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: רַב עִילִישׁ גַּבְרָא רַבָּה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Responds to the document in step 21 by assuming it must describe a permitted deal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Because רב עילִישׁ was a great man, the document must describe a permitted arrangement.

steps.title: Either way: half the profit means two-thirds of the loss
steps.stepSummary: רבא begins a two-sided argument: if the deal gave half the profit, then the loss must have been split two-thirds to one-third.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whichever way you look at it: if it was half in the profit, then it was two-thirds in the loss.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא starts a "whichever way" argument to show the document left something out. This is the first half of the argument, and it continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the worker really got only half the profit, the deal could only be permitted if the investor carried more of the loss, two-thirds of it. That extra share of the loss is the worker's payment for his effort. So the document's "half in the loss" cannot be the full picture.

keyTerms.meaning: Whichever way you look at it

phrases.english: Whichever way you look at it:
if it was half in the profit,
then it was two-thirds in the loss,

steps.triggerLanguage: מָה נַפְשָׁךְ? אִי פַּלְגָא בַּאֲגַר – תְּרֵי תִּילְתֵי בְּהֶפְסֵד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins proving רבא's claim from step 22 that the document must have meant a permitted deal.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A half-profit deal is only permitted if the loss is split two-thirds to one-third.
